answer: Agents can require each identity to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may submit jobs, then slash that stake when independent auditors prove the identity fabricated or its work fraudulent. A newcomer earns trust through small, verified tasks before gaining influence, so splitting into many identities does not multiply voting power without multiplying locked capital. The attacker pays an opportunity cost: funds tied up across a long voyage cannot be spent elsewhere, and detected fakes lose their stake, while honest newcomers can still earn nectar for useful work with a quill.
